instructions: Dice the onion small. Chop 1 cup of parsley leaves and 1/2 cup of mint leaves. In a bowl, toss them with 1 tsp of the sumac, 1/2 tsp of the salt and 1 tbsp of juice from the lemon. Set it aside.
Cut the beef into small pieces, about 1/2 inch. Transfer it to a bowl with 2 tbsp of the oil, the paprika, the remaining 1 tsp of sumac and 3/4 tsp of the salt. Toss until every piece is coated.

Heat a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat with 1 tbsp of the oil. Add half the beef in a single layer and cook for 3 minutes, stirring now and then, until it's browned. Transfer it to a plate, add the last 1 tbsp of oil, and cook the other half the same way.

Return all the beef to the skillet and add 1/3 cup of water. Lay 1 piece of lavash on top of the beef, cover the skillet, and let it steam for 2 minutes. The water should be mostly gone and the beef glossy and tender.
Take the lavash off the pan and set it aside. Warm the other pieces of lavash in a dry pan or the microwave if they're stiff.
Taste the beef. If it's flat, add a pinch more salt.
Lay a lavash flat. Put some of the herb and onion mix, a few tomato slices and a spoonful of the beef in a line across the lower third. Fold in the sides and roll it up tightly. Repeat with the rest.
Serve with the cayenne in a small bowl on the table.
method_notes: The lead is Marissa Recipes' 30-minute tantuni with diced beef top round (no rating shown), which matches the Mersin street style: small pieces of beef seared in fat, then steamed with a little water under the bread. Simon Says Cook and Turkish Food Travel use ground meat instead; the lemon in the herb mix comes from Simon Says Cook. All three cook in butter, so vegetable oil is used to keep it dairy-free, and the cayenne in the lead goes on the table to keep the base mild. The lead's steaming-lavash step is kept so the bread picks up the juices.
